entries.title: US: Award-winning Kashmiri filmmaker detained
entries.summary: Arfat Sheikh was detained by ICE agents in Washington on September 24, it was confirmed on Wednesday. Officials say he "illegally overstayed his lawful admittance" as US President Trump pursues an immigration clampdown.
entries.content:
United States of America

US: Award-winning Kashmiri filmmaker detained

October 8, 2026

Arfat Sheikh was detained by ICE agents in Washington on September 24, it was confirmed on Wednesday. Officials say he "illegally overstayed his lawful admittance" as US President Trump pursues an immigration clampdown.

A filmmaker whose award-winning work has explored conflict in his native Kashmir has been detained by United States immigration officials on suspicion of residing and working in the country illegally.

Arfat Sheikh was detained by US Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) after disembarking a flight from California at Washington Dulles International Airport on September 24, according to a statement from friends and relatives who labeled his detention "unlawful" and are calling for his release.

The Department of Homeland Security (DHS), which oversees ICE, confirmed to the Reuters news agency on Wednesday that Sheikh had "legally entered the US on a temporary basis and illegally overstayed his lawful admittance."

Sheikh, 42, entered the US in 2019 on a student visa and enrolled on a graduate course in film studies at Georgia State University, according to the statement from friends and family.

Having applied for asylum in 2020, the statement said he had a ​pending immigration application and was authorized to work and live in the US. It did not mention the ground for asylum.

The DHS said Sheikh would receive due process but that a pending ​application does not confer legal residency status.

ICE arrests up amid Trump immigration crackdown

US President Donald Trump has been pursuing an immigration crackdown and deportation drive that he claims is aimed at improving domestic security.

His administration said in August it was to "identify ⁠and revoke the non-immigrant visas of foreigners who have come to the US claiming to be short-term visitors, but then file for asylum to stay here permanently."

The number of ICE arrests hit record levels this summer, with about 51,000 recorded across August.

Critics say the crackdown has violated due process and ​free speech rights and ​has created an unsafe ⁠environment, particularly for ethnic minorities, who have raised concerns about racial profiling.

Sheikh, who hails from India-administered Kashmir, won the Emerging Filmmaker Activist Award at the Teaneck International Film Festival in 2025.

His first feature film, 2024's "Saffron Kingdom," won Best Feature Film at the Chicago Filmmakers Awards, ​the LA Film and Documentary Awards, the Melbourne Independent Film Festival and the ​Wake Forest ⁠Film Festival.

The film explored conflict in Kashmir, a disputed Muslim-majority region claimed by both Hindu-majority India and Islamic Pakistan, which each control only part of it and have fought wars over it.

Edited by: Rana Taha

entries.title: IMF reaches tentative $1.21 billion bailout deal with Pakistan
entries.summary: Pakistan's dependence on Gulf energy imports, remittances and regional financing has left the economy exposed to the fallout from the Middle East conflict.
entries.content:
October 8, 2026

Pakistan's dependence on Gulf energy imports, remittances and regional financing has left the economy exposed to the fallout from the Middle East conflict.

The International Monetary Fund (IMF) has reached a staff-level agreement with Pakistan that could unlock about $1.21 billion (roughly €1 billion) in financing, the lender said on Wednesday, as the South Asian country grapples with spiking food and fuel prices, and high unemployment.

The bailout deal still needs to be approved by the IMF Executive Board.

IMF negotiator Iva Petrova said Pakistan had successfully navigated the impact of the Middle East conflict, with strong policies helping preserve macroeconomic stability.

How does the Middle East conflict impact Pakistan?

Pakistan's economy grew 4% in the first three quarters of fiscal 2026 with full-year growth estimated at 3.6%, the IMF said.

Petrova attributed the weakened momentum to "higher energy prices and supply disruptions."

Inflation eased to about 10.3% in September after peaking in May, while core inflation remained contained, Petrova said.

Pakistan remains dependent on external financing to shore up foreign exchange reserves and meet debt repayments.

A prolonged Middle East conflict makes it particularly vulnerable due to its dependence on Gulf energy imports, remittances and financing from the region, according to S&P Global Market Intelligence economist Ahmad Mobeen earlier this year.

In the recent past, Pakistan has had to turn to the IMF to tackle Islamabad's acute balance-of-payments crisis.

Edited by: Rana Taha

entries.title: Brazil: Thousands of students march against Bolsonaro
entries.summary: After Flavio Bolsonaro came out on top in the first round of Brazil's presidential election, thousands of people joined student-led protests against the far-right in Rio de Janeiro.
entries.content:
Brazil

Brazil: Thousands of students march against Bolsonaro

October 8, 2026

After Flavio Bolsonaro came out on top in the first round of Brazil's presidential election, thousands of people joined student-led protests against the far-right in Rio de Janeiro.

Thousands of people joined a student march in Rio de Janeiro, Brazil, on Wednesday to protest the possibility that Flavio Bolsonaro could become president after the far-right candidate came out on top in the first round of the country's presidential election on Sunday.

Bolsonaro, the son of jailed former President Jair Bolsonaro, won about 2 million more votes than the incumbent president, the left-leaning Lula da Silva.

But since neither reached the 50% hurdle to win the presidency, the pair will face off in a run-off on October 25, in which Bolsonaro is considered the favorite.

"If Bolsonaro wins, Brazil will become a colony of the United States," said 20-year-old literature student Joao Victor Vieira, voicing the fear of many on the left in Brazil that Bolsonaro is too ideologically aligned with US President Donald Trump.

Brazil: 'Never again Bolsonaro'

Other marchers held signs with messages such as "Brazil isn't anyone's backyard," "I don't vote for someone who sells Brazil," and "Never again Bolsonaro" – all against a soundtrack of drums, fireworks and chants.

"We're fighting for Brazil, not for Lula," said Talita Amaral, a 19-year-old environmental sciences student, wearing Brazil's iconic yellow and green football shirt, often worn by nationalist Bolsonaro supporters but which opponents have been aiming to reclaim for themselves.

"We don't have time to be sad, we need to be doing this, occupying the streets, sending messages in WhatsApp groups, trying to convince people," she told the Associated Press.

For Alice Carneiro, a 25-year-old maritime shipping administrator, the prospect of another Bolsonaro conjures fears of far-right policies which will discriminate against Brazil's minorities – such as her transgender wife.

"I'm here because I believe in democracy," she told the AFP news agency. "Because I'm scared."

Witnesses reported that the march was notably more crowded and animated than President Lula's rally on the same street on Friday, the culmination of a lackluster campaign ahead of the election.

After the third, fourth and fifth places all went to right-wing candidates, who polled over eight million votes between them, Lula and the left appear to have a mountain to climb in the run-off.

The incumbent's campaign has shifted its focus to social media, where the far-right dominates but Lula has largely been absent, arguing he "like[s] to say only what is essential." But on Wednesday, the president convened leftist influencers who won legislative seats on Sunday to advise his campaign.

Edited by: Rana Taha

entries.title: Christa Pike 'angry and confused' after botched execution
entries.summary: Pike's lawyers have said she was very aware of Tennessee's failed execution effort. A judge has ordered state officials to preserve all evidence from the botched execution.
entries.content:
October 7, 2026

Pike's lawyers have said she was very aware of Tennessee's failed execution effort. A judge has ordered state officials to preserve all evidence from the botched execution.

A US judge told the state of Tennessee to preserve all evidence related to the failed attempt to execute Christa Pike, who lawyers say is "angry and confused" after waking up in hospital nearly a week after the ordeal.

Pike, who was sentenced to death for torturing and killing classmate Colleen Slemmer in 1995, survived despite being given two lethal doses of pentobarbital, a lethal injection drug.

What do we know about Christa Pike's current state?

One of her attorneys spoke about the 50-year-old's state after the failed execution.

"She is angry and confused about everything right now," Randy Spivey said during a news conference, adding Pike is "very aware" of what was done to her.

"She cannot move either of her arms, both of her arms and hands are tremendously swollen, and we do not know what, if any, function she will regain in her arms," Spivey said, adding that "there's a long road ahead" for her recovery.

Pike is the only person known to have survived after receiving lethal injection drugs, according to the Death Penalty Information Center.

Luke Ihnen, another lawyer for Pike, said that "medical staff have asked that the shackles be removed and have been denied that request."

Her lawyers continue to demand that Tennessee Governor Bill Lee commute Pike's sentence to life in prison and never reattempt her execution. The Republican governor had denied a clemency appeal two days before the failed execution.

Pike's recovery period unclear

Experts say it is possible that the failed execution was due to a problem with the IV line that caused the injection to pool in her tissue rather than enter her bloodstream.

"Apparently at no point did any member of the execution team realize that the IV lines were not correctly placed or that the veins had blown," her attorneys wrote in their court filing.

Pike's arms were burned and blistered due to the injection, according to her legal team, who are demanding that the prison authority holds all information from the attempted execution, including needles and execution logs.

It is not yet clear how Pike's recovery might unfold and whether she will be subjected to another execution attempt.

Edited by: Rana Taha

entries.title: As US midterm elections loom, Trump's campaign tactics are becoming increasingly unusual, and expensive
entries.summary: Despite not being on the ballot, Trump is campaigning hard ahead of the upcoming midterm elections. His tactics and promises have mostly been at the expense of US taypayers. Experts say some might violate federal law.
entries.content:
United States of America

US midterms: Is Trump campaigning at taxpayers' expense?

October 7, 2026

Despite not being on the ballot, Trump is campaigning hard ahead of the upcoming midterm elections. His tactics and promises have mostly been at the expense of US taypayers. Experts say some might violate federal law.

It's neither a joke nor fake news but a real report from earlier this week: Donald Trump has backed down. On Monday, the US president announced that a series of advertisements aired in September promoting him and his administration would no longer be funded with taxpayer money. 

"The radical Left is upset with the fact that I am taking ads, which I consider to be a positive promotion for our great USA, and paying for them with USA money," Trump wrote on his platform Truth Social.

He went on to claim that funding partisan ads with public money was a "rather standard thing to do," before adding that future ads would be paid with money raised from donations.

The ads themselves have caused some controversy in the United States. They ran in September between popular shows such as Saturday Night Live and football games, marked with the line: "paid for by the US government" — that is, paid with tax dollars.

The commercials showed scenes such as when US troops captured Venezuelan President Nicolas Maduro earlier this year but they mostly consisted of images and videos of Trump himself, along with combative messages that he would "expel the warmongers" or "throw off the sick political class," and ensure that the US did not become a communist state. 

Public funds for personal praise

Political opponents and a series of NGOs responded to the campaign with sharp criticism. Not only does US law prohibit the use of taypayer funds for political advertisements, but the ads also appeared shortly before the midterms — elections held near the midpoint of a president's four-year term.

On Tuesday, the US broadcasting network CBS reported that, according to contracting records, the US Department of Homeland Security had paid an agency $20 million (€17.9 million) for a "national media campaign."

The "rather standard" practice that Trump referred to actually applies to public service announcements, but this is not what the campaign ads are, argued the US non-profit consumer advocacy group Public Citizen.

"Federal law explicitly prohibits using appropriated public funds for government propaganda, self-aggrandizement, or partisan political advertising," the organization wrote in a public complaint to the Federal Communications Commission (FCC) ."Yet, that is exactly the nature of Trump's recent campaign ads."

Independent experts have also voiced concerns. Patrick Malone, a professor in the department of Public Administration and Policy at American University in Washington DC, said the timing of the videos was problematic.

"You're not supposed to use taxpayer dollars to pay for anything that's campaign-related," he told DW. "Technically, [Trump] is not campaigning. He's not saying 'Vote for me!' The thing that's created the challenge here is the timing. Weeks before the midterms, this is a real big issue."

Will the Republicans keep their majority after midterms?

Voters do not choose presidents in the midterm elections but members of Congres, which comprises the Senate and the House of Representatives and is the legislative branch of the federal government. On November 3, those eligible to vote will cast their ballots for all the seats in the House of Representatives, and roughly a third of the seats in the Senate. Some states will also be choosing governors.

Republicans have not been faring well in recent polls, which may be why Trump has been trying to promote his party's achievements. The Republicans currently hold a majority in both houses, with 53 of 100 seats in the Senate, and 219 of 435 seats in the House of Representatives. This has enabled Trump to pass a large number of his proposals fairly easily.

But a Reuters/Ipsos poll released on Monday indicates that this could soon change. "Voters age 50 or older preferred Trump's party over the Democratic Party by just 2 percentage points — 44% to 42% — compared to an 8-point Republican advantage in December," it found. This age bracket "is particularly important for midterm elections, when older Americans historically have made up large shares of the electorate."

Meanwhile, among voters under the age of 50, "Democrats led by 18 points," the survey showed.

The poll also found that opinions on Trump himself were low, with "32% of Americans giving a thumbs up to Trump's presidency." This level of approval, the study highlighted, was unchanged from an earlier poll "that saw the leader's rating at the lowest of his political career."

Republicans shy away from Trump's support

This could also be one of the reasons why Republican candidates do not seem so keen on making public appearances with the president, usually a highlight of a campaign trail.

Many US citizens associate Trump with high living costs, or the war with Iran, which has dragged on for over half a year now.

One Republican operative told the news website Politico on condition of anonymity that if the the president were to visit a battleground state — where Democratic and Republican support is fairly equal among voters — to campaign for his party, they suspected their "candidates would come down with COVID" to avoid having to attend.

In September, a number of Republicans skipped Trump's big party convention — typically reserved for presidential, not midterm elections — even though the event could have offered them a platform for their campaign.

Susan Collins from Maine and Dan Sullivan from Alaska, are just two examples of Republican senators whose seats are on the line and who did not attend. Neither did candidates for the House of Representatives from the swing states Arizona, Iowa and Michigan.

Trump promises $5,000 payout if Republicans win

Those who skipped the event missed the president repeating an unusual campaign message: To encourage more people to vote, Trump urged supporters to "pretend" he was on the ballot.

And if that wasn't enough, he also promised each US citizen eligible to vote a $5,000 payout if Republicans maintained their majority in both houses of Congress.

Keeping that pledge could cost the federal government over $1.2 trillion, but observers doubt it would ever come to that.

"He has no money to do that with. It would have to be authorized and appropriated by Congress," Mallone explained. "I think the likelihood is very slim," he added. "It's one of those things like 'Mexico is going to pay for the wall.'"

Whether Trump's commercials or promised payouts will be enough to rally majority Republican support remains to be seen.

This article was originally published in German.

entries.title: Evicted Spanish pensioner who sparked housing protests has died, Madrid tenant union says
entries.summary: Maricarmen ⁠Abascal, the octogenarian woman whose eviction set off housing protests across Spain, has died, a tenants' union in Madrid has said. Unions are now calling for a nationwide general strike on November 11.
entries.content:
Spain

Evicted Spanish woman who sparked housing protests has died

October 7, 2026

Maricarmen ⁠Abascal, the octogenarian woman whose eviction set off housing protests across Spain, has died, a tenants' union in Madrid has said. Unions are now calling for a nationwide general strike on November 11.

Maricarmen Abascal, the 87-year-old woman at the center of the nationwide protests in Spain due to her eviction from her Madrid home, has died, the local tenants' union said.

"We are sorry to announce that Maricarmen passed away today," the Madrid Tenants' Union said in a statement, adding that Abascal's cause marked "a turning point in the history of this country."

Who is Abascal and how did she spark Spain's protests?

Abascal was evicted from the home where she lived her whole life on a stretcher after the company owning the apartment drastically increased the rent.

She had been hospitalized after the eviction took place due to exhaustion as an agreement with her home's owners was reached.

The Madrid Tenants' Union said the solution came "too late," labeling the ordeal "totally avoidable" and "torturous" for the 87-year-old.

Prime Minister Pedro Sanchez sent his condolences to Abascal's family after learning of her death.

"I send hugs to all of those who mourn this loss as if it was their own," Sanchez posted on his X account.

Voicing his sadness over Abascal's death, Spanish Minister for Territorial Policy Angel Victor Torres said she symbolized the plight of many people struggling with the country's housing crisis.

Spain's unions call for general strike

Spain's trade unions called on Wednesday for a nationwide general strike on November 11 over housing issues.

The UGT and CCOO unions urged the population to "mobilize for better salaries, for decent housing and for price controls in the face of inflation that undermines our purchasing power."

The strike "is the response to the insatiable real estate greed that speculates with one of the public's main rights, making access to a decent home practically impossible,", they said in a statement.

The nationwide protests triggered by Abascal's eviction and lawmakers' rejection of housing reforms intended to help tenants led Sanchez to call for early elections on November 29.

Sanchez, of the Socialist Party, is looking for a shift in the public narrative after his government's handling of the migrant crisis in Ceuta, as well as alleged corruption among his party's ranks.

entries.title: Saudi Arabia, Pakistan, Turkey: Could the Mecca defense pact become a game changer in the war against the Houthis in Yemen?
entries.summary: Pakistan and Turkey have agreed to provide "practical measures" to defend Saudi Arabia against Houthi attacks. Could a new alliance reshape the war against the Houthis in Yemen?
entries.content:
Middle East

Pakistan, Turkey boost role in Yemen's Houthi-Saudi conflict

October 7, 2026

Pakistan and Turkey have agreed to provide "practical measures" to defend Saudi Arabia against Houthi attacks. Could a new alliance reshape the war against the Houthis in Yemen?

The latest iteration of Saudi Arabia's defense deal with Turkey and Pakistan, the Mecca Joint Defense Agreement, is taking shape amid the country's escalating conflict with Yemen's Houthi militia.

According to the trilateral defense commitment, which was signed by Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman, Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdogan and Pakistani Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif on August 7, 2026, an armed attack on any one of the three states involved should be regarded as an attack on them all.

Yet, despite ongoing Houthi attacks on Saudi Arabia and Saudi attacks on Houthi militants in Yemen, neither Pakistan nor Turkey had joined Saudi Arabia's combat operations since the deal was signed, arguing that the command and operational structures were still being developed.

But since Monday, the situation has changed after an emergency meeting between Saudi Arabia, Pakistan and Turkey's defense and foreign ministers and senior military chiefs in the Saudi capital Riyadh. According to a joint statement, Turkey and Pakistan decided to implement the collective defense commitments in practical terms immediately. This means providing military forces and capabilities and ensuring their rapid deployment in Saudi Arabia. The appointment of a retired Pakistani lieutenant general, Nauman Mahmood, as the alliance's first secretary-general was also announced. He will serve a three-year term.

"Ankara and Islamabad undoubtedly will seek to strengthen the Saudi kingdom's posture vis-a-vis the Houthi threat and demonstrate that the Mecca agreement can pass its first real test and show up as a game-changing alliance," Burcu Ozcelik, a senior research fellow for Middle East security at the London-based Royal United Services Institute, told DW.

"However, what the activation of the Mecca pact means operationally, including the specific capabilities deployed and the scope of their missions, has not been made public," she said, adding that this was "not unusual for such a military operation amid myriad sensitivities."

According to the 2026 Global Firepower military strength ranking, Saudi Arabia, Pakistan and Turkey between them have about 1.4 million active personnel, some 3,400 military aircraft, 6,000 tanks and more than 340 naval assets.

On Wednesday, Saudi Arabia intercepted another ballistic missile north of Riyadh. Earlier this week, Saudi-backed Yemeni government forces had launched a large-scale offensive, to recapture territory along the Red Sea coast around the strategic Bab el-Mandeb Strait and the city of Mokha. Saudi Arabia launched airstrikes to support the offensive.

Turkey considers a solution through dialogue

The scope of a potential Turkish military deployment remains unclear. Turkey is a NATO member, which means that any military involvement on its part could carry broader implications for the entire military alliance.

Turkish Foreign Minister Hakan Fidan noted after the meeting in Riyadh on Monday that there were not only military options on the table. "We also discussed what could be done to resolve the problem peacefully and through dialogue,"

Turkey's involvement in the Mecca defense deal has been criticized by opposition parties in the country. Under Turkey's constitution, international agreements generally require approval by the Grand National Assembly of Turkey but this has not yet been granted.

"How can the so-called Mecca agreement on joint defense be valid and implemented without having been submitted to the Turkish parliament for approval?" Namik Tan, an Istanbul lawmaker from the social democratic Yeni Parti and a former Turkish ambassador to Israel and the United States, asked in a statement.

Yani Bagcioglu, a retired Turkish admiral, also warned that "the risk of Turkish forces and commercial vessels linked to Turkey becoming targets of Houthi attacks should not be overlooked."

Pakistan's tightrope walk amid the Iran war

The third signatory, Pakistan, is walking its own particular tightrope. On Monday, Defense Minister Khawaja Muhammad Asif told Pakistani television channel Geo News that Pakistan and Turkey were playing a "supportive role," with their forces involved in "reconnaissance and other things," while Saudi forces were engaged in combat.

"Pakistan's contribution to the defense of Saudi Arabia is nothing new," Imtiaz Gul, an independent Pakistani security analyst, told DW. "The arrangement has existed for six decades," he said, adding that "defense against the Houthis nevertheless represents a different kind of challenge because the group is considered an Iranian extension and by implication, Iran would consider this an attack on its regional interests."

A direct engagement in Yemen at Saudi Arabia's side would, therefore, risk not only ending Pakistan's apparent neutral status as a mediator in the US-Iran war, but also strain relations with Tehran, he said. He pointed out that Saudi Arabia was a close ally of the US, while the Houthis are backed by Iran. 

Hisham Al-Omeisy, a Yemeni conflict analyst in Washington, told DW that "for years, a cornerstone of the Houthi narrative and rallying cry has been a fight against perceived external enemies." Accordingly, he added, foreign boots on the ground in Yemen would "not only backfire, it would solidify the Houthi local coalitions and fuel their recruitment drives."  



Haroon Janjua in Islamabad contributed to this article.

Edited by: Anne Thomas

entries.title: Russia: WHO not able to 'fully' assess plague situation
entries.summary: The UN health agency said Russia should be more transparent about the case of the plague as reports of a second case of the disease emerged. Russia played down any concerns, saying the population faces no risk.
entries.content:
October 7, 2026

The UN health agency said Russia should be more transparent about the case of the plague as reports of a second case of the disease emerged. Russia played down any concerns, saying the population faces no risk.

The World Health Organization (WHO) said it could not fully assess the situation of  the suspected plague death of a laboratory employee in Russia.

"We don't yet have the full picture of this event and we're not able to conduct a full risk assessment," WHO chief Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus said.

Kremlin spokesperson Dmitry Peskov played down the reports as "false information," insisting only Russian authorities' official statements should be relied on.

What has Trump said about the suspected plague situation?

Peskov also said he had no information regarding a planned call between US President Donald Trump and Russian President Vladimir Putin about the situation, despite Trump announcing such a call was scheduled.

Trump said the death of the technician did not appear to be linked to a biological weapon.

"We're going to find out soon, but we don't think so," Trump told reporters, adding that Russia claimed the incident was under control.

The US did make a formal request for more information on the matter from Russia, the AFP news agency reported.

Second suspected case reported

This comes after a 28-year-old female technician employed at a plague research institute in the Irkutsk region of Siberia died of the disease, possibly contracting it from a broken test tube.

According to the WHO head, Russia should clarify reports of a "second employee with pneumonia of undetermined cause" at the institute.

While the United States, the European Union and the WHO have all called on Moscow to be transparent about the case, Russian authorities insist the population in the region is safe.

"There are no epidemic risks for the population," the country's health agency said, adding its investigations had resulted in "no emergencies" and emphasizing the plague research institute's compliance.

"More than 90% of contacts have completed medical observation," the agency added. "The results of almost 5,000 laboratory tests did not reveal any dangerous pathogenic microorganisms."

In response to the reports, Mongolia said it implemented "health surveillance and monitoring measures" at the border between the two countries.

Pneumonic plague is a highly contagious bacterial infection of the lungs which can pass from person to person through the air, for example, via coughing.

Edited by: Sean Sinico

entries.title: German politicians warn of antisemitism on October 7 anniversary
entries.summary: Leading German politicians including Chancellor Merz and President Steinmeier called for people to reject antisemitism.
entries.content:
Germany

Politicians warn of antisemitism on October 7 anniversary

October 7, 2026

Leading German politicians including Chancellor Merz and President Steinmeier called for people to reject antisemitism.

High-ranking German politicians marked the anniversary of the terrorist attacks that took place in Israel on October 7, 2023.

German Chancellor Friedrich Merz spoke about doing more to fight antisemitism within Germany, while also pressing for a two-state solution between Israelis and Palestinians.

"We are witnessing rising antisemitism in Germany — antisemitism that far too often goes unchallenged," Merz said, adding that his government "will do everything" to combat it.

"Jewish people must be able to live without fear throughout Germany," Merz said in a statement, also emphasizing Germany's support for Israel. "Our Israeli friends can count on our commitment to ensuring that such a crime never happens again."

'Political action' needed

German President Frank-Walter Steinmeier said antisemitism in Germany "flared up in an intolerable manner since October 7."

"Germany must continue to stand up against antisemitism and for Israel’s security, for the dignity and self-determination of the Palestinians, and for the prospect of peaceful coexistence in the Middle East," he said in a statement.

Federal Parliamentary Speaker Julia Klöckner commemorated the day by emphasizing that more needs to be done to combat antisemitism through "political action."

"Antisemitism should not be allowed to have a place on our streets or our political debates," she said.

Germany stands with Israel

Some 1,200 people were killed in the attack, carried out by Palestinian militant group Hamas and its affiliates, while 251 people were kidnapped to Gaza, in the deadliest attack on Jews since the end of the Holocaust.

More than 74,000 people have been killed in the Gaza Strip in Israel's war following the attack, with some countries and human rights groups saying Israel is committing genocide against Palestinians.

Demonstrations were held across Germany for victims of both the Hamas attacks and the Israeli war that followed.

In Berlin, a crowd of around 1,700 people, many waving Israeli flags, gathered at Bebelplatz, according to police estimates. Israeli Ambassador Ron Prosor and German Interior Minister Alexander Dobrindt also attended. Bebelplatz was the site of Nazi book burnings following the party's seizure of power in 1933.

Dobrindt called antisemitism a "poison" that threatened to infect parts of society, adding, "We must clearly and consistently stand against it every day."

Germany has supported Israel throughout the war, although Merz did halt of delivery of some military equipment to Israel following growing legal concerns over the war in Gaza, including arrest warrants issued by the International Criminal Court (ICC) against Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and then-Defense Minister Yoav Gallant.

Although Germany is a party to the treaty that created the ICC, Merz vowed not to arrest Netanyahu should he travel to Germany.
